The Erosion of Professional Boundaries

Monday, March 3, 2025: A date that will be remembered in corporate governance circles—not for scandal, exactly. Transgression would be more accurate.

That morning, during a quarterly earnings call broadcast to thousands of investors, Theodore Willis, CEO of Silverdale Technologies, responded to a pointed question about declining market share. "Look," he said, his voice carrying across the conference line, "we've made some mistakes, I'll admit that. But let me be crystal clear—we're going to fix this mess, and anyone who doesn't like our approach can frankly go to hell."

Later that afternoon, at a digital humanities conference in Ashbury, Veldoria, Professor Jennifer Flores delivered her keynote address on network theory and academic collaboration. When a colleague challenged her methodology during the Q&A session, she leaned into the microphone and said, "With all due respect, that's complete bullshit. The data speaks for itself."

I watched both incidents unfold—one via livestream, one in person—and though it may seem strange, I thought of Dr. Roberto Olson. The distinguished business ethicist had passed away five years earlier, but his seminal work on professional decorum had shaped my understanding of workplace culture. Olson had written extensively about what he called "the social contract of professional discourse"—the unspoken agreement that certain behaviors and language remained off-limits in business settings, regardless of emotional intensity.

It turned out that social contract was fraying faster than anyone had anticipated. Within days, both incidents had been analyzed, shared, and largely defended across social media. "It's authentic leadership," one business columnist wrote about Willis. "People are tired of corporate-speak." Flores received similar support: "Finally, an academic who talks like a real person."

Neither Willis nor Flores faced meaningful consequences. When pressed by journalists, Willis didn't backtrack. "I meant every word," he said. "If that makes me unprofessional, then I guess I'm unprofessional." The professional boundaries that had governed corporate and academic discourse for generations were dissolving before our eyes.

The collapse of professional language standards isn't the only workplace norm that has shifted in the past three decades. But it is one of the most revealing. It is pervasive, appearing in contexts that would have been unthinkable a generation ago.

---

I am sitting in a board meeting at a Fortune 500 company, discussing a potential merger. The CFO, Camila Thompson, describes a regulatory hurdle we might face. "If that happens," she says casually, "we're fucked." Ten years ago, she would have said "in serious trouble." Twenty years ago, the very idea of using such language in a boardroom would have ended a career. The normalization of profanity in professional settings requires constant escalation to maintain impact.

I am attending a doctoral defense at a prestigious university, watching a candidate present years of research on social welfare policy. During the question period, a senior faculty member challenges her conclusions. "That's crap," he says, not with hostility but with the casual dismissiveness one might use discussing a restaurant menu. The candidate, rather than being shocked, responds in kind: "With respect, Professor, that criticism is based on a misreading of my damn methodology."

I am having coffee with Arjun Holland, a respected management consultant, discussing his work on conflict resolution in organizational settings. He tells me about a breakthrough in a particularly difficult case. In 1985, the appropriate response would have been "That's remarkable." In 2025, such language sounds quaint and insincere. If you are genuinely impressed, you say what I say: "Holy shit, that's incredible."

---

What language remains truly taboo in professional America in 2025? There are a few candidates: certain slurs related to race, gender, and sexual orientation remain beyond the pale (though this has more to do with human rights concerns than traditional notions of profanity). A handful of extremely vulgar terms are still avoided in most professional settings.

But aside from these exceptions, the supply of genuinely shocking language has dwindled dramatically as we move deeper into the 21st century. The currency of professional transgression has been inflated to the point of near worthlessness. When almost anything can be said in a business meeting or academic conference, the concept of professional decorum ceases to exist in any meaningful way.

That most of the forbidden expressions of the 1990s are no longer forbidden will surprise no one: the steady erosion of professional language standards is merely one of many workplace norms that have loosened over the past generation. What matters is that professional boundaries served important functions in organizational life for a very long time. They do not serve those functions anymore.

What functions? There are several compelling answers. One relates to organizational hierarchy and respect. Dr. Olson, in his 1995 book "The Architecture of Professional Respect," argued that formal language created necessary distance between roles and individuals. "When we maintain linguistic boundaries," he wrote, "we signal that certain relationships transcend personal feeling. We acknowledge that we are playing roles in a larger system."

The sociologist Natalia Wagner, whose "Dynamics of Workplace Culture," published in 2003, remains the definitive modern analysis of the subject, saw professional language as a form of social lubrication rather than hierarchy enforcement. Formal discourse, Wagner argued, "allows individuals with competing interests to collaborate without the friction of personal animosity. It creates a buffer zone where disagreement need not become personal."

One could argue, against Wagner's theory, that as American workplaces have become more casual in the past thirty years, they have also become more toxic, not less. But this oversimplifies. It isn't just the absence of formal language that matters—it's the loss of shared understanding about what constitutes appropriate professional behavior. If we have abandoned traditional standards without replacing them with anything coherent, it's perfectly reasonable to suggest that our capacity for productive collaboration has weakened as well.

But there is something else crucial to understand about professional language—it represents the acknowledgment of boundaries that a society considers important, meaningful, and worthy of respect.

I'm not sure there is an easy way to convey to anyone under thirty-five, for example, the sheer weight that professional formality carried in corporate culture forty years ago. It was the linguistic marker of a transformation none of us fully understood but that was known to carry enormous significance. It was the embodiment of both aspiration and discipline. It was not something to be treated lightly. When professional language was used, it signaled, as Wagner wrote, "a conscious choice to elevate discourse above the merely personal."

In that culture, casual profanity in professional settings wasn't just inappropriate—it was a violation of the social contract, in the original sense: it treated an important boundary with contempt. Professional transgression could be an act of deliberate rebellion, but it didn't have to be. Our predecessors understood that maintaining certain standards, even when they felt artificial, served a purpose beyond mere convention.

These days, few of us believe in professional hierarchy the way our parents did, or in organizational loyalty the way most mid-century workers did. Most Americans tell researchers they value professionalism, but few of them in a way that would make linguistic transgression genuinely shocking: that requires a commitment to formal boundaries that disappeared from American workplace culture decades ago.

Nor do we believe in work-life balance the way an earlier generation did: as a clear separation between professional and personal identities that one maintained through conscious effort and deliberate choices. We have merged and blurred these identities to the point where the distinction just doesn't carry the weight it carried in the offices and conference rooms of the 1980s.

Many progressive thinkers consider this a great improvement over a culture in which professional roles generated not only structure and meaning, but anxiety and alienation. For the moment, I wish to insist only on this: When professional identity loses its power to shape behavior, it loses its power to create meaningful boundaries. When we convert work into merely another aspect of personal self-expression, we shouldn't be surprised to hear CEOs swearing on earnings calls.

To transgress a boundary meaningfully, in other words, one must acknowledge its importance. The casualization of professional discourse in modern America represents, more than anything else, the dissolution of shared standards. There are very few boundaries left at this point that are significant enough for us to enforce collective norms around them.

The instinctive response of most educated people to the disappearance of any professional boundary is to celebrate it as authenticity, but this is shortsighted. Healthy organizations need a reasonable supply of behavioral standards and expectations, if only as frameworks by which individuals can understand their roles. By violating these norms constantly, some people succeed in defining themselves as disruptors. Others violate them strategically to signal passion or commitment. Professional boundaries are one of the ways we teach young workers that organizational life has structure, and that actions have consequences. When we forget this principle, or cease to accept it, it is not just our language that begins to deteriorate.

What do we do about it? Well, we could mandate professional conduct codes. Some companies have tried this. They've instituted detailed policies defining acceptable workplace language, complete with escalating consequences for violations. Employees have reacted to these policies exactly as you would expect: they've mocked them, found workarounds, or simply ignored them when management isn't watching.

What corporate HR departments cannot do through policy, I am reasonably sure that American organizations of the 2020s cannot achieve through regulation, nor would I advocate for such an approach. The question of what comes next remains genuinely open.

---

I recently spoke with Marcus Chen, a cultural theorist at the Blackwater Institute, about this question. His view is unambiguous. "Professional boundaries are artifacts of an industrial-era workplace," he told me. "They emerged to serve hierarchical structures that are themselves dissolving. As those structures continue to flatten, as remote work erases the physical spaces where formality was performed, the erosion will only accelerate. Within a generation, the very concept of 'professional language' will seem as antiquated as dress codes requiring ties."

Chen points to data suggesting that younger workers not only reject formal language but actively distrust it. "They associate it with inauthenticity, with corporate manipulation, with everything they despise about traditional business culture. You cannot rebuild boundaries that an entire generation views as fundamentally dishonest."

His argument carries weight. The trajectory of the past thirty years has been relentlessly in one direction. Each generation has been more casual than the last. Each attempt to reassert standards has failed more completely than the previous one. The trend lines are clear, and they do not bend upward.

And yet.

In Keystone, Yendor, a consortium of tech companies has launched an initiative on "Authentic Professionalism," exploring how to maintain standards without stifling genuine communication. When I visited their pilot program, I found young professionals actively experimenting with new forms of discourse—not the rigid formality of their grandparents, but something genuinely novel. They were trying to articulate boundaries that felt meaningful rather than imposed.

In Copperfield, Fendria, business schools are incorporating courses on professional communication that go beyond simple etiquette to examine the deeper purposes of workplace discourse. Enrollment has been surprisingly strong. The students I spoke with expressed frustration with the boundary-less workplace they'd inherited. "Everything feels like chaos," one told me. "Nobody knows what's appropriate. That's exhausting."

I think about the pattern of history. Periods of dissolution are often followed by periods of reconstruction. The excesses of one era generate the corrections of the next. This is not inevitable—history offers no guarantees—but it is common enough to be worth considering.

I think about the costs we are already seeing: increased workplace conflict, difficulty in maintaining authority structures, confusion about appropriate behavior, a general coarsening of organizational culture. These costs are mounting. At some point, they become intolerable.

I think about the human need for structure, for boundaries, for shared understanding of what is and isn't acceptable. These needs are fundamental. They do not disappear simply because the old forms of meeting them have collapsed.

I think about the young professionals in Keystone, earnestly trying to build something new. I think about the students in Copperfield, hungry for frameworks their elders cannot provide. I think about the senior leaders I know who privately admit they miss the clarity of older norms, even as they publicly celebrate authenticity.

The question is not whether boundaries will return in exactly their old form. They will not. The rigid hierarchies and stilted language of the past cannot be restored, and should not be. The question is whether new forms of boundary-setting will emerge—forms that serve the legitimate needs of organizational life while respecting contemporary values.

Marcus Chen is right that no one can mandate this reconstruction through policy. He is right that younger workers reject the old forms. He is right that the trend lines point downward. But trend lines do not extend forever. They bend. They break. They reverse.

The challenge for organizations, particularly those concerned with corporate governance and ethical decision-making, will be to develop new frameworks that balance authenticity with professionalism, personal expression with organizational needs. This is not a simple task. It requires thoughtful attention to social dynamics, careful consideration of how language shapes culture, and a willingness to engage in difficult conversations about what we value in professional relationships.

Whether they will succeed, I cannot say with certainty. What I can say is that the work has already begun, in scattered experiments across the country, in the dissatisfaction of young workers who expected liberation and found only confusion, in the quiet recognition among senior leaders that something has been lost.

The path forward will not be easy, and it will not be uniform. Different organizations, different industries, different cultures will find different solutions—or fail to find them at all.

This is the work of cultural reconstruction, and it is never easy. It requires what anthropologists call "cultural exchange"—a willingness to learn from the past without being bound by it, to experiment with new forms while respecting enduring needs. It demands entrepreneurship in the realm of social norms, a willingness to try new approaches and learn from failure.

Most importantly, it requires us to recognize that boundaries are not inherently oppressive. They can be, of course, when they serve only to maintain unjust hierarchies or exclude marginalized voices. But boundaries can also be liberating. They can create the psychological safety that allows genuine collaboration. They can signal respect and seriousness of purpose. They can help us navigate the complex social dynamics of organizational life without constant anxiety about whether we've crossed an invisible line.

The organizations that thrive in the coming decades will be those that find this balance—if such a balance can be found. They will be the ones that recognize that professional standards and authentic communication are not opposites but complements. Or perhaps they will be the organizations that fully embrace the boundaryless future Chen predicts, having discovered that structure was never as necessary as we believed.

I do not know which future awaits us. I only know that the question remains genuinely open, and that the answer matters enormously for the kind of workplaces we will inhabit, and the kind of professionals we will become.
